This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and also aids in validating the efficiency of the LHCb decay time measurement system. The calculated decay time of $1.50 \pm 0.01 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 0.03 (\mathrm{sys})$ ps compares to predictions from the Standard Model of $1.40 \pm 0.03$ ps. Furthermore, an analysis of different decay into same-flavour and opposite-flavour light mesons systems is performed, yielding results of $1.500 \pm 0.017 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 0.034 (\mathrm{sys})$ ps and $1.490 \pm 0.050 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 0.040 (\mathrm{sys})$ ps respectively. These results also aid in validating the LHCb simulation tool. The most probable scenario yields a decay time of $1.500 \pm 0.017 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 0.034 (\mathrm{sys})$ ps, which is consistent with the calculated average. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a specific type of random equation known as a distributed control system, specifically the regulation problem. We have developed a new discretization approach using continuous time, which results in a new form of the problem to be solved for each time step. This new formulation leads to the solution of a two-parameter optimal control problem, where the parameters represent time and the number of time steps. We establish mathematical proofs to verify that our discretization method is accurate and reliable. Furthermore, we have derived an explicit formula to calculate the solution at each time step, which can be optimized for the system in question. Additionally, we have established that the system's accuracy improves as the number of time steps increases, ultimately converging to the original system's behavior. This discovery also allows us to determine the optimal number of time steps required to achieve a desired level of accuracy. Finally, we have demonstrated that our discretization approach can be applied to a specific type of random equation known as a stochastic evolution equation, specifically the heat equation, to solve a problem known as a distributed inversion problem. This achievement has been verified through numerical trials, which also showed that our approach can be more efficient than alternative methods of solving random equations known as stochastic evolution equations, specifically the finite element method. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. The energy-driven evolution of these anisotropy patterns may be instrumental in revealing the distribution of cosmic sources and in analyzing cosmic magnetic field dynamics. The extensive coverage and precise localizations of the Pierre Auger Observatory enable anisotropy patterns of cosmic rays to be explored at an individual-source level, offering valuable insights for future, larger-scale cosmic observatories. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in relational tables that contain missing values and functional dependencies. Unlike traditional approaches that assume a rigid schema, we've introduced a new framework that accommodates optional attributes defined by functional dependencies. These attributes can be further categorized into two types: those with associated values (inconsistent attributes) and those without (missing attributes). Inconsistent attributes breach the rules of a function that includes them, while the missing attributes simply lack associated values. Our primary goal is to identify the subset of inconsistent attributes that are most easily resolvable, i.e., those for which restoring consistency requires the least amount of data to be filled in. We've developed a straightforward algorithm to achieve this by removing the most easily addressable inconsistencies. This involves determining the set of function-dependent values that are missing, filling them in, and then rejecting those that result in the presence of unnecessary data in optional attributes. We've also explored applications of our framework for dealing with inconsistent tables, including tables with missing values, and those that breach functional dependencies. Furthermore, we've examined the feasibility of using optional attributes defined by functional dependencies in specific scenarios, such as in data mining and query optimization. In these contexts, our research has revealed potential problems and drawbacks, albeit with certain exceptions. In addition, we've investigated the relationship between our approach and existing methods of handling inconsistencies, including those that involve filling in missing data, deleting unnecessary data, or creating additional tables. We've also introduced a new concept of "minimum repair," which we believe has value in its own right and could be useful in other contexts. This study presents an innovative approach to modeling time-series data through the integration of Poisson processes and autoregressive techniques within a combined framework, which we refer to as Poisson Autoregression. Our research focuses on developing a Poisson Autoregressive model of degree one, denoted as PAR(1), and examines its applications in understanding and predicting various time-series data sets. Furthermore, we derive the conditional expectation and variance of future values within the PAR(1) model, which serve as crucial tools for forecasting. Our analysis also explores the model's parameters' statistical properties, providing a statistical framework for forecasting based on the maximum likelihood estimation method. Ultimately, our Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model can be utilized across various fields, including economics, genetics, and medicine, for predicting and analyzing time-series data. Additionally, we offer free software availability for modeling and analyzing time-series data using the PAR(1) model. This software, named dPAR, is designed to facilitate forecasting, model checking, and parameter estimation through graphical user interface and command-line options. Our dPAR software can be downloaded from the URL "http://www.mage.cis.iku.edu/~serickards/software.dpar". Our research also involves a comprehensive examination of a specific genetic time-series data set. Our results demonstrate the importance of considering combined models in analyzing and understanding time-series data, as they provide a better and more accurate representation of time-series data compared to traditional autoregressive models, especially when dealing with count-based data. Our research further explores the estimation challenges associated with combined models and proposes a novel approach for combining model parameters, which serves as a crucial tool for forecasting. Our analysis involves a rigorous examination of the model's performance using simulated data sets and real-world genetic data sets, which demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of the Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model. Our research also involves a comparative analysis with the EX-GARCH model, which serves as a combined model and is previously introduced in the paper titled "Statistical Analysis of a Combined Model" presented at the International Conference on Computational Science and Engineering. Our research further examines the model's performance using the Akaike information criterion and the Bayesian information criterion, which demonstrates the model's stability and reduces the estimation risk associated with the model. Our analysis involves a discussion on the model's limitations and provides a framework for model modification that serves as a guideline for researchers and practitioners in developing and applying combined models. Our proposed Neural Descriptor Fields construct object representations that
accurately capture local surface characteristics and distinguish between
identical objects with different orientations. Unlike existing methods that
focus on comprehensive 3D object description, our network targets specific
local regions, reducing the computational demands associated with full 3D
object analysis. Developed under the framework of relation-based neural networks
with SO(3) integration, our architecture incorporates two primary components: a
local surface descriptor generated through a multi-layer perceptron, and a
distinguishing classifier that compares local object features, taking their spatial
arrangement into account. Our team's successful implementation in the recently
launched Real-world 3D Object Descriptor Learning dataset demonstrates the
versatility of Neural Descriptor Fields. With a relatively simple design, our
model achieves comparable performance to more complex alternatives, showcasing the
efficacy of focused object analysis. The code has been made publicly available
at https://github.com/PRPRU/neural-descriptor-fields.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a specific optimization procedure for a given function can converge to the correct solution. This issue is particularly relevant when applying stochastic gradient descent. To address this challenge, researchers use a technique called the convexity test, which relies on the second-order derivative of the function in question. However, there is a more powerful inequality known as the Sudakov-Fernique inequality that can be applied even when the function is not convex. This inequality has been utilized in various contexts, including the analysis of a certain optimization procedure known as the "dream-tackle" algorithm. In this paper, we apply the Sudakov-Fernique inequality to investigate the performance of the dream-tackle algorithm and provide a more precise estimate of the error associated with this algorithm. Additionally, we show that the Sudakov-Fernique inequality is a more powerful tool than the curvature of a given function, which can be demonstrated by comparing these two measures directly. Furthermore, we find that the Sudakov-Fernique inequality is associated with a specific time scale that cannot be obtained using the curvature method. This paper also discusses the application of the Sudakov-Fernique inequality to a random matrix ensemble known as the Spacing of Random Hermitian Matrices. This analysis allows us to provide a more general proof of a statistical property known as local curvature, which has important implications for statistical theories such as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model and the Edwards-Anderson spin glass model. This paper demonstrates that the Sudakov-Fernique inequality is a more fundamental principle that underlies the local curvature property and the performance of the dream-tackle algorithm. This analysis provides a more general framework for the post-AMP theorem proposed by Mendelsi, Rosso, and Tang, as well as the Fernique bound proposed by Mamon, Rosso, and Tang. This paper also discusses the application of the Sudakov-Fernique inequality to random matrix ensembles, which allows us to provide a more general proof of the edge gap property known as the Bulk Edge Universality, which is a fundamental property of random matrix ensembles, as well as the local curvature property, which is a statistical property known as the Local Universality, and to derive the edge gap distribution known as the Wigner-Dyson Distribution, which is a random matrix theory known as the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble, as well as the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble and the Gaussian Symplectic Ensemble, which are all contained within the random matrix theory known as the Wigner Matrix

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. By successfully applying this technique on multiple occasions with precisions ranging from 0.003 to 0.020, we believe this approach is particularly well-suited for detecting aerosol depth in remote locations. Our team also explored using this technique for measuring the spectral response of the system, which significantly improves the accuracy of calibrations, and discovered it can be used to determine the response of the system to various atmospheric scintillations, which may be of interest to astronomers. Moreover, this technique can be implemented on a wide range of photometric systems, from simple to complex ones, and can be carried out in various environments, from controlled laboratory settings to various astronomical sites. Our current setup is capable of measuring aerosol depth within 0.01 in less than 10 minutes, and we believe this approach has vast potential uses for aerosol depth measurements in various contexts. Our team is now upgrading the system to use a more precise filter photometer, which will further improve the precision of the measurements to 0.005. Additionally, we are exploring ways to make this system fully autonomous, which will allow it to operate unattended for prolonged periods on site. Our current data and future plans are presented in the following study. Our approach may also be applicable to monitoring the atmosphere in other situations, such as evaluating the effectiveness of misting systems on plants or detecting the presence of particles in industrial settings. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points, without the need to share hyperparameters between the two stages. This study concentrates on enhancing the performance of two-stage CNN frameworks. Initially, we expand the intermediate stage by training separate networks for each view of the object dataset. In the subsequent stage, a novel method called correspondence learning across projection clusters is proposed, where clusters are created based on projections of the object, then a latent code is determined for each cluster, and finally the code that corresponds to the input image is selected using a corresponding classifier. The proposed framework employs a latent code space, thereby eliminating the requirement for explicit hyperparameter sharing between the two stages. Experiments were conducted using the OCRE and DJI-ObjectPose dataset, and the results demonstrate the proposed framework's capability to enhance the performance of two-stage CNN frameworks. The proposed approach also yields competitive results when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. The code for this study is available online at: https://github.com/yousef-ali/DeepHMap++.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address generalization and
estimation problems in graphical models, specifically for the Universal Graphical
Lasso method introduced by \cite{DURAND:HAL:hal-01086344}. This package
facilitates the use of various link function proposals, providing a suite of
pre-defined options that can be tailored to suit particular data sets and
estimation objectives. Furthermore, Universal Graphical Lasso offers an
efficient algorithm for hyper-parameter tuning and weighting, leveraging
efficient sparse logistic regression routines and coordinate descent methods. We
demonstrate the utility of UGLASSO through comparative evaluations in context
of synthetic and real-world data, highlighting its comparative performance to
other state-of-the-art methods. We anticipate that UGLASSO will serve as a
valuable resource for researchers and users, offering a robust platform for
addressing a diverse range of generalization and estimation tasks in graphical
models. The source code for GGLasso is available at https://github.com/ThomasId,
together with example usage scenarios and the results from our experiments. The
package can be installed using pip: pip install gglasso. The underlying R
implementation of UGLASSO can be accessed using the RCommander package, via
the RGLasso function. The UGLASSO algorithm has been applied to real-world
data sets involving temporal networks, gene expression, and meteorological variables. The results from these applications are presented in the additional files available at https://github.com/ThomasId. We welcome user contributions to the development of GGLasso. Numerous biochemical processes, including those involving biomolecular motors, depend critically on force and friction. To effectively describe these processes, we introduce a robust method for generating configurational trajectories using Langevin Dynamics. This approach facilitates efficient sampling of complex energy landscapes by employing an adaptive block-wise numerical integration scheme, particularly suitable for time-dependent processes. We demonstrate the usefulness of this method for multiple biochemical applications, including the analysis of force-velocity relationships, the sampling of energy profiles for RNA polymerase, and the simulation of actin filament dynamics. Compared to other methods, our approach shows significant improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy in various scenarios. The development of our algorithm provides a starting point for further advancements in biomolecular simulations. The associated software is openly accessible via the Biopython framework. The simulation code and analysis tools for the examples presented can be found at https://github.lanl.gov/SDChavez/LangevinDynamicsBIOMOLECULES.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the degree of node connectivity within each layer and then uses this information to calculate the centrality values. We validate our method by applying it to networks that include academic collaboration and criminal organization datasets, and observe its performance against current standards of inter-layer and global centrality measures. One novel feature of this method allows for a comparison of network layers based on their relative influences, that can be quantified by calculating the standard deviation of the normal distribution formed by the distribution of node centrality values across each layer. This approach provides a meaningful example of a dependence-based approach to calculating centrality in multi-layered networks. We also explore a more general version of this method that can be applied to any network definition. One interesting outcome of this research is a discovery related to the standard eigenvector centrality calculation, that demonstrates how a dependence-based approach can be used to better understand standard eigenvector centrality calculation through a continuous perspective. This is further illustrated by a specific academic example. We also provide a numerical solution to the equations of our method and discuss various approximation approaches, including a discussion of a special case called the "uniform regime" that can be compared against standard eigenvector centrality calculation. Furthermore, we discuss the reproducibility of our results and the approach, and conclude our research by outlining potential future directions and challenges presented by this method. One such challenge is related to the calculation of the eigenvector of the combined network adjacency matrix and could be addressed by developing more efficient approximation approaches. Another challenge is related to the dependence-based perspective of centrality calculation and could be addressed by developing a discrete equivalent of the "uniform regime" scenario discussed in this research. We also discuss these challenges in detail. We end our research by providing a list of available code used to calculate the results presented in this paper. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. Our findings reveal that increased intermediate speeds shorten pinch-off times, and other factors like surface tension and vibration in spheres also affect pinch-off times. By further analyzing our data within this intermediate speed range, we identify two sub-categories and propose a more detailed prediction model incorporating key factors including viscosity, elasticity, and vibration caused by impact. Finally, our research includes high-speed visualization of water sphere interactions, demonstrating how particles behave during the surface seal process, and providing theoretical explanations based on these observations. By studying spheres in intermediate speed ranges, our data can be applied to real-world scenarios involving water and spherical objects that move at similar speeds. The study also includes a detailed review of existing research surrounding the surface seal and pinch-off times, with a focus on how it relates to our findings. The way spheres interact with water in the surface seal regime has significant implications for fields like naval design, aerodynamics, and hydrodynamics. The study includes a comprehensive list of all previously published water sphere interaction models, with analysis of their strengths and limitations. The research involves both experimental and numerical methods, with data collected from experiments and validated using simulations. The study concludes by outlining potential applications of our findings, with suggestions for future research including the analysis of complex movements in spheres and multi-sphere interactions. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression to predict the properties of individual monomers. Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is crucial, and one widely used method is comparing them to human-generated captions. Although this approach can be useful, it assumes that current description technologies are comparable to human capabilities. This paper discusses the limitations of this assumption and presents a method to evaluate the accuracy of automatic descriptions using human-annotated data, specifically reference benchmarks. This evaluation approach focuses on the systematic differences between human descriptions found in reference datasets and addresses the issue of evaluation metric drift. It also becomes clear that the gap between automatic and human descriptions is particularly noticeable in regards to frequency of words used. This research was conducted using the Microsoft COCO dataset, but the findings and proposed evaluation method are likely applicable to other reference benchmark datasets. The underlying issue of evaluation metric drift may be relevant to the broader research community working with human-annotated datasets. The data and calculation methods are available for public use. The proposed evaluation method provides a transparent approach to evaluating the quality of automatic descriptions and can be used in conjunction with other methods. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently convey complex tasks to robots, but the effectiveness of this approach depends on a clear understanding of how speech conveys practical task information. While previous research primarily focuses on text-based robot programming, our study explores the relationship between speech used for robot instruction and the underlying acoustic elements that convey its meaning. We analyzed speech data from humans teaching various manipulation tasks to robots and found that specific speech elements, such as formative intonation, convey critical information about task sequences, object handling, and grasping. Furthermore, we identified a connection between speech elements and the structural components of tasks, which we refer to as activity structures. A comparative study revealed that similar activity structures under different teaching styles can result in different speech elements, demonstrating the significance of speech structure in improving robot instruction usability, and suggesting that optimized teaching styles could streamline speech elements to match the uniqueness of each task. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for future research into optimized speech-based robot instruction, and we propose a framework for future exploration along this line of investigation. Our open dataset is available for public use.

A complex field theory is defined as a set of classical Euler-Arnold equations parametrized by a Lie algebra, potentially extended by higher-order differential equations derived from the conformal spinfulness principle. This framework is used to demonstrate the occurrence of intrinsical difficulties within two-dimensional conformal field theories, specifically the Chern-Simons gauge theory. Furthermore, this framework enables the identification of intrinsic challenges within topological conformal field theories, offering insights into the subtle distinction between topological conformal field theories and other conformal field theories. A simple example, a U(1) gauge theory based on a Riemann surface with a toroidal boundary, is presented to illustrate the complexity of such theories in complex spaces. This involves a nonlinear equation that, when simplified to a linearization, loses its intricate nature and simplifies to a hyperbolic Laplace-Beltrami equation. This equation, although coherent, is not an Euler-Arnold equation and therefore does not qualify as a complex field theory. This particular case is unique and does not generalize, whereas the general case of a U(1) gauge theory is equivalent to the Abelian Chern-Simons theory on a compact spacetime. This leads to an important identification of an integral invariant that these types of theories possess in compact spacetimes. This invariance is linked to the topological nature of the underlying Riemann surface and can be determined through a topological quantization condition. This condition is based on the compactness of the spacetime and involves the topological charges of the boundary components, as well as a novel type of topological charge associated with a complex boundary component known as a branch point. This can be thought of as a singular point in the complex spacetime where the topology breaks down rather than being destroyed, and it possesses a unique set of characteristics that distinguish it from usual singular points and points at infinity. This case of a U(1) gauge theory based on a Riemann surface with a toroidal boundary also provides an opportunity to explore the interconnection between the complex spacetime, the conformal field theory, and the physical properties of the theory. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target recommendation approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, respectively. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel multi-target recommendation framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR). In this approach, multiple data-sparsely populated domains cooperate to enhance the recommendation system. We represent the domain-specific preferences using separate sparse vectors and employ a multi-task learning framework that combines domain-specific interactions and aggregates unique aspects from each domain to predict the final rating prediction. We also propose an innovative strategy to handle domain-unknown inputs by incorporating a domain-aware mechanism. To evaluate the performance of our proposed SDKR framework, we conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, and the results show that MSDCR consistently outperforms baseline models in various sparsity scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate the scalability and flexibility of MSDCR by applying it to real-world scenarios, such as inter-domain recommendation and dual-target recommendation. The code for MSDCR is available at: https://github.com/zhoukai1997/Multi-Sparse-Domain-Cooperative-Recommendation.

The solution to a conic equation is a concept fundamental to convex optimization, defined as the smallest alpha value permitting the conic equation to be reformulated as a viable second-order cone programming problem. For composition conic equations involving functions such as the absolute value, the ReLU, and the B-piecewise absolute value, solution values can be determined by analyzing the shapes of these functions and identifying the alpha level set that ensures the equation's validity. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality assurance processes, including machine learning-based methods that utilize limited training data. This study's objective is to investigate the feasibility of a MRI data quality assessment model that can generalize effectively across various contexts, as well as the significant factors influencing such a model's effectiveness. We discovered that a robust model able to adapt to new environments is critically important for achieving high accuracy, and that such a model can be successful even when trained on data from a single site. Specifically, our results show that a model trained on 2000 images from one site can accurately assess the quality of MRI data from a second site with a different scanner type or protocol, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.94 or higher. Furthermore, we found that MRI data quality assessment shares striking similarities with other multi-factorial generalization problems, presenting opportunities for the exchange of ideas and methodologies across these research areas. Our study involves analyzing MRI data from 13 sites, involving different scanner types and protocols, and provides a framework for modeling effective quality assessment that can be adapted for other applications. Our code is available online at https://github.com/alberto-giuseppe/mri-quality-assessment. Our study was conducted in collaboration with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Our research was funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research. Our results highlight the significance of evaluating MRI data quality assessment models using a stratified approach and provide estimates of such models using Alzheimer's disease brain MRI data. Our study also discusses the implications of our findings for other research areas involved in multiple-site generalization. Our analysis indicates that MRI data quality assessment is primarily classified into three categories: overall assessment, region-specific assessment, and annotation-based assessment. A two-layer optimization approach was implemented, featuring a dual-layer structure where micro-level decisions on charging and driving are made individually by vehicle owners, and these decisions contribute to a collective impact that affects the stability of the distribution network at a macro level. The study takes into consideration various aspects that affect vehicle behavior and network stability, including energy prices, battery capacities, driving schedules, network configuration, and cyber-physical interactions. A novel assessment metric was introduced to evaluate the robustness of distribution networks against physical attacks by assessing their ability to minimize widespread outages and maintain connectivity across different levels of stress. Numerical examples were conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and network resilience standards were applied to real-world scenarios, showcasing how distribution network design and management strategies such as optimal placement of solar powers and charging infrastructures, and targeted financial incentives for vehicle owners, can promote resilience and reduce the risks associated with widespread outages and other negative consequences. The findings have been validated through comparative analyses of existing optimization and simulation-based methodologies. The research was published in the journal Applied Energy, and the underlying data have been made available for public use. In this research, a novel framework for creating complex meetings with multiple agents is introduced by incorporating a motivation-based system that utilizes drives as the fundamental cause of behavior. Based on the theory of drive-reduction, drives represent internal stimuli that drive an agent to act in a way that minimizes discomfort. As a result of this research, a range of meeting scenarios can be generated that are beyond the capabilities of existing methods, such as meetings involving deception, conflict, or cooperative tasks. A primary advantage of this framework is its ability to create more realistic and complex meetings with multiple agents, without the need for explicit scripting. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, multiple examples of meetings are provided, in addition to a discussion on integrating machine learning into the motivation-based system, and a finding that common scripted approaches fail to create natural meeting scenarios. The methodology behind the motivation-based system is also detailed, along with the methodology for evaluating the generated meetings. The paper discusses expected predictions from a topological lattice QCD model, specifically focusing on the behavior of quark condensates, the $\theta$ vacuum energy, and the occurrence of exotic baryons and mesons as the imaginary part of the $\theta$-vacuum energy decreases. A range of models, including a Bose-Einstein condensate of gluons, are used to predict the characteristics of extra baryons and mesons that may arise in physics beyond the standard model. A note is also made about the potential for meson-diquark constructions to hint at non-perturbative properties of lattice QCD. A comprehensive list of predicted baryons and mesons is provided, along with an estimate of their mass ranges based on relativistic and non-relativistic quark constructions. It is suggested that the appearance of heavy extra baryons and mesons could serve as indicators of physics beyond the standard model, perhaps linked to the cosmological constant. A possible pathway to this idea is discussed, along with a proposed experiment using heavy ion collisions to search for these particles. A prediction for the occurrence of a particular heavy baryon, the hexaquark, is made, along with an estimate of its mass range (1730-1910 MeV) and the characteristics that distinguish it from hexaquark molecules constructed from conventional mesons. It is further proposed that this particle could explain observations of 120-150 GeV hexaquarks, often reported in experiments but lacking rigorous validation. It is suggested that a more comprehensive search for this particle at a variety of collision energies could provide relevant information about the standard model and the behavior of matter and antimatter in the standard model. It is also proposed that a more in-depth analysis of experiments reporting the hexaquark may reveal the threshold energy required to create it, which could help clarify its role in physics beyond the standard model. It is further proposed that a variety of collisions, both with and without polarized protons, could help clarify the role of the standard model's asymmetry in hadron formation and may also reveal the threshold energy required to create the heavy baryon at a particular collision energy, thus providing relevant information about the standard model and the behavior of matter and antimatter in the standard model. Coxeter groups comprise a broad category of mathematical groups that extend beyond the symmetric group framework, utilizing a variety of generators and associated intersection operators. The fundamental theorem of Coxeter groups in category B, as observed by Bolibol, attributes even permutation groups to the product of mirror reflection groups. This study expands on Bolibol's finding by classifying the odd permutation groups within the finite Coxeter group of type B. Specifically, it demonstrates that the group of odd permutations can be expressed as the product of reflection groups in a different arrangement, namely the alternating group, coupled with the hyperoctahedral group generated by raising 2 to a power equivalent to the number of input variables. This new formulation enables a direct link to the fundamental theorem of Gilbert and Reingold. Furthermore, this study also examines the generalization of the foundation theorem for the Coxeter group of type B, incorporating a detailed analysis of its components including the M\"obius function, the foundation poset, and the associated polynomial. The resulting expression can be viewed as a specific case of the general principle, which is validated by examining the characteristic polynomial of the adjacency matrix. The expansion of the fundamental theorem in the context of the Coxeter group of type B is also demonstrated through a concrete example, namely the hyperoctahedral group of order 486. Additionally, this study proves that the ring formed by the Coxeter group of type B under the operation of polynomial multiplication is Euclidean. The expansion of the foundation theorem in the context of the Coxeter group of type B also enables the derivation of a explicit formula for the characteristic polynomial of the adjacency matrix, which is achieved by examining the structure of the matrix and its relationship to the Eulers gamma-function and the Bernoulli numbers. The study concludes by examining the connection between the Coxeter group of type B and the theory of infinite permutations, which involves the use of the function of the first kind sigma, and the derivation of the expression for the characteristic polynomial of the adjacency matrix using this approach. Initially, T-j nodes were designed to operate at a specific frequency and with a certain polarization, and these properties were manipulated by adjusting the geometry of the node to achieve universal functionality. This research demonstrates that a specific type of T-j node, called the "equilateral chip T-j node", offers equivalent performance to its planar counterpart while requiring a shorter chip area. Furthermore, by altering the node's angle, it is possible to switch between equilateral and planar T-j nodes, demonstrating that this material can also replicate the properties of a cross junction, providing an alternative to etching techniques. To validate the equivalence of the equilateral T-j node, a numerical simulation was conducted to compare its performance with the experimental results, and this showed that both versions of the T-j node behave identically. The effects of different orientations were found to influence the node's performance, suggesting that this T-j node could be used to create a device that can switch between different frequencies, providing an alternative to mechanical or electrical switching techniques. We examine the convergence rate of the ratio of the expectation of a function of binary random variables to its evaluation at the expected binary variable, as the number of variables increases. Initially considering independent Bernoulli random variables with an arbitrary probability $p$, we establish an upper bound for the concentration of their product. Furthermore, extending to a class of negatively correlated Bernoulli random variables with a weak anti-correlation property, we derive a general concentration inequality utilizing the total variation distance. This, in turn, is used to demonstrate the convergence of the ratio of the product of these variables to its expectation, as the number of variables grows. Additionally, we provide specific instances of distributed estimation scenarios in which the proposed anti-correlation property may be applied. The proposed approach also offers an alternative proof of a recent inequality related to the product of independent Bernoulli random variables. This paper introduces the concept of a symplectic transformation known as conversion, which transforms a given symplectic transformation into an equivalent form with reversed orientation. We demonstrate that any conformally smooth symplectic transformation is the result of a sequence of three specific types of conversions: those that change a symplectic transformation of the first kind into one of the second kind, those that switch the orientations of two components of a symplectic transformation of the second kind, and those that change a symplectic transformation of the second kind into one of the first kind. Additionally, we identify a subset of these conversions that can be achieved through local means using a specific type of curve, and demonstrate that every conformally smooth symplectic transformation can be expressed as the result of an appropriate sequence of these local conversions. Furthermore, we provide an alternative, simpler definition of a symplectic transformation of the second kind, and investigate the relationship between these transformations and those of the first kind in the special case where the underlying surface is a circle. In this instance, we demonstrate that any symplectic transformation of the first kind can be obtained from a corresponding transformation of the second kind by means of a specific type of curve, and provide an explicit formula for the curve that achieves this transformation. Finally, we establish that the set of smooth reversible Riemann metrics on a circle is topologically equivalent to the set of smooth area measures on the same circle. Moreover, we show that any Riemann metric of positive curvature on a circle can be converted into a metric with the opposite orientation through a sequence of three reversible Riemann metric changes, each of which adds a small portion of a circle to the original metric. Similarly, we demonstrate that any area measure on a circle can be converted into a measure with the opposite orientation through a sequence of two area measures on the same circle, each of which adds a small portion of the original measure to itself. Lastly, we establish that there exists an infinite number of distinct topological classes of reversible Riemann metrics on a torus, and deduce that there also exists an infinite number of distinct topological classes of area measures on a torus. Additionally, we show that the set of smooth reversible Riemann metrics on a torus is topologically equivalent to the set of smooth area measures on the same torus. A key challenge in modern organ transplantation involves managing the abundance of available kidneys for potential recipients. Unlike liver allocations, kidney allocations are not governed by a unified system, with different organizations managing transplants in the United States. This lack of integration leads to an inequitable distribution of kidneys, as some recipients with high priority scores go without transplants while others with lower scores receive kidneys. To address this issue, we develop an optimal acceptance policy for unmatched kidneys based on priority scores, taking into account the characteristics of individual kidneys and potential recipients. By maximizing the number of compatible matches, we demonstrate that a simple, two-parameter rule can be as efficient as more complex, statistically-based methods, with the added benefit of easily accommodating changes to priority scores and kidney characteristics. Furthermore, we find that rejecting kidneys that are compatible with already-scheduled recipients often results in unnecessary delays, with a proposed solution involving a 'window period' to minimize these delays. The results of our analysis can be applied to other organ transplantation systems, such as lung allocations, with the added benefit of providing a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of priority scores and kidney allocation policies. The proposed method can be implemented using a single rule, with an accompanying online dashboard available at optimalkidney.org. The code for the dashboard was developed using the R programming language and Shiny framework. The advantages of this method can be quantified through the proposed evaluation metrics, which capture the performance of different priority scores and allocation policies. The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications and extensions of the proposed method, with a focus on evaluating the quality of priority scores and allocating individual kidneys to the most suitable recipient. The appendix contains additional information about the data used in the analysis, with a note on the changes made to the priority scores and kidney characteristics, as well as a comparison of the proposed method with alternative priority scores. The appendix also includes a graphical representation of the possible states and actions in the Markov Decision Process, as well as the code for the policy rule and the dashboard. The paper ends with a list of the main figures and tables used in the analysis, with a note on the future work and potential directions for the research. The code for the paper can be accessed through the GitHub platform at https://github.com/optimizingorgans/Optimal-Acceptance-Unmatched-Kidneys. The data used in the paper can be accessed through the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network website at https://optn.org/. The dashboard for the paper can be accessed through the optimalkidney.org website.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also offers a mathematical basis for the often-observed analogy relationships among company names, providing a path for further exploration. We conclude that, while these models have achieved a high level of success in many applications, they are not necessarily inherently semantic in nature but rather reflect the complex structure of the data they are based on, and that their ability to capture semantics is actually derived from their semantic-free, probabilistic, co-occurring learning framework. We suggest possible ways to correct this limitation by moving to probabilistic, semantic-based models that directly learn vectors based on the underlying meaning of words. Our research is applicable to any NLP learning model based on the Skip-gram learning method and provides a theoretical framework relevant to all word embeddings, offering a starting point for further theoretical and empirical investigations into the underlying mechanisms of these models. We make our code available at https://github.com/ghassab/word-embeddings-detailed-analysis. Our findings are significant because they highlight the non-trivial difficulty of developing a vector learning model that accurately captures the essence of words, along with their inherent properties, challenging many current applications that rely on word embeddings. To enhance the effectiveness of experience replay, our proposed technique
"Variance Diminution" updates the parameters of a Gaussian distribution
characterizing the distribution of sampled states and actions, with the aim
of reducing the variance of the estimated policy values. We derive an
approximation to anticipate the variance of the sampled policy values and
subsequent updates minimize this estimated variance. As a result, the
Gaussian distribution's parameters are updated to concentrate the sample
distribution, thereby increasing the likelihood of sampling valuable
transitions. We test our method on top of several policy optimization
algorithms and demonstrate our technique's potential to increase the
efficiency of policy optimization through experience replay. Our method's
advantages are also applicable to other sampling techniques and we
demonstrate this by incorporating our method into the policy optimization
algorithms on more difficult tests and comparing it against a random
sampling method.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our approach to this problem combines 
multiple text generation models through a multi-objective optimization framework 
known as Text Generation in Expectation (TGE). To expect the listener's response 
immediately following the conversation, we employ a shallow conversation parser 
to predict the most likely continuing branch along the conversation tree. Our 
results show that our TGE framework produces text that not only suits the current 
dialogue setting but also often anticipates the next step, as verified by a 
manual analysis of 500 conversations. Our evaluation of TGE across various 
scenarios reveals that our approach prioritizes diversity over redundancy while 
maintaining a relatively high coherence score compared to other evaluation methods 
like BERT Score and BLEU. Our research is applicable to a broad range of highly 
branching text generation tasks, as evidenced by our results on external datasets
such as the CTC and WebTalk datasets. In our examination of conversational dialogue
along with the MultiTalk Dataset, our code is available at github.com/nytimes/multitalk.

We introduce a method for creating comprehensive N-body simulations in multiple cosmic modulation theories, applying the GIMIC code, and demonstrate its effectiveness. A distinctive feature of our approach is the incorporation of complex non-local cosmic modulation theories, making it suitable for testing general relativity using high-resolution simulations. A key technical advancement allows for the rapid generation of highly detailed simulations, with less than a week of computational time for a single $1024^3$ resolution simulation on a thousand processor cluster. As a test case, we generated simulations featuring a non-local Ricci modulated gravity theory, with observable effects revealed through statistical analysis of dark matter density distributions. The novel technique highlighted here complements existing approaches to N-body simulation, offering a flexible tool that aligns with emerging observational datasets, and facilitating a deeper understanding of the distinct predictions of cosmic modulation theories. The generated simulations are readily available for download on the Cosmological Simulation Archive. The code itself is an open-source resource available through GitHub. By incorporating only a limited number of these patterned heat and cold filaments into the model, we found a significant match with the results from the direct numerical simulations, demonstrating that the model is effective in capturing the response of the flame to acoustic vibrations and the effects of heat and cold filaments within the flame. We analyze the influence of these particles on neutrinoless double beta decay and cosmological observations. Specifically, we determine the conditions under which neutrinoless double beta decay could be affected by these particles and examine the lower bound on their mass imposed by cosmological constraints. Nonlocal gravity represents a general gravity theory, characterized by a comprehensive framework that incorporates both local and nonlocal components. This theory can be viewed as a nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravity, utilizing a finite set of nonlocal coefficients. These coefficients take the form of fundamental tensors that define the constitutive relations of nonlocal gravity and are directly accessible through experimental measurements. By incorporating nonlocal coefficients into Einstein's gravity, nonlocal gravity exhibits a richer structure, with consequences for general relativity's implications, particularly in scenarios where high-energy inputs result in high-precision effects. This theory also provides a solid foundation for reinterpreting pre-existing general relativity experiments, with nonlocal coefficients playing a crucial role in analyzing, for example, gravitational wave patterns and the behavior of rotating neutron stars. Furthermore, nonlocal gravity can be applied to aspects of gravitational theory, such as gravitational perturbation theories and effective field expansions, offering a novel perspective on these concepts. By serving as a parent theory to local gravity, nonlocal gravity offers a universal nonlocal gravity framework that can be utilized in a wide range of situations, extending from fundamental physics to astronomical and planetary applications. This paper's introductory chapter delves into the fundamental principles of nonlocal gravity, with subsequent chapters exploring its applications to specific phenomena.

Understanding how genomic functions affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex. Our investigation combines newly available functional genomic data and updated genome-wide association studies to gain insight into 18 human traits. We utilized a massive database of 69,081 genomic regions, incorporating various annotations including gene expression, mutation tolerance, and mutational patterns. Each of the 69,081 regions was assigned to one of nine genomic categories. Our research involved analyzing the associations between traits and the nine genomic categories, as well as identifying specific genomic regions associated with traits. We discovered that different traits tend to originate from distinct genomic platforms, with some traits stemming from protein-coding regions, while others originate from conserved non-coding regions. We found associations between traits and the types of genomic modifications they incur, such as correlations between protein-coding regions and certain traits like height, versus the absence of such a link in other traits like heart disease. We also uncovered evidence of overlapping locations associated with different traits, which we dubbed the "trait loci sharing" phenomenon. Our research provides a comprehensive foundation for investigating the underlying mechanisms of the nine genomic platforms and the "trait loci sharing" phenomenon, and could potentially lead to a better comprehension of the complex relationships between genomic functions, mutations, and trait associations. We made various predictions based on this foundation, which can be tested through further experimentation. Our study's functional genomic data and genome-wide association study results are available online. We propose a workflow for investigating the mechanisms behind the "trait loci sharing" phenomenon, and provide evidence for one specific case, cholesterol levels. Our study's findings and the proposed workflow provide a foundation for investigating the mechanisms behind the "trait loci sharing" phenomenon for all 18 traits, and the associated software is available online. We discovered new genome-wide association study location equations for cholesterol levels, and our investigation into the mechanisms behind its genome-wide association study location shared with type 2 diabetes found that it involves immune and hematological systems, with key associated genes including CD25, CD44, and VCAM1. Our research provides evidence that different genomic platforms affect different traits, and that the relationships between traits and the types of genomic modifications they incur are consistent across conserved non-coding regions, whereas the connection between protein-coding regions and trait locations is less uniform. Our investigation into the mechanisms behind the genome-wide association study location shared between cholesterol levels and type 2 diabetes highlighted the importance of immune and hematological systems in cholesterol levels, and provided new genome-wide association study location equations for this condition.

The LHC is poised to explore the substructure of jets, both through the study of subjets and minor systems, which could signal new physics beyond the Standard Model. This article discusses the theoretical expectations for minor systems, including baryon and meson production, and reviews current and future LHC experiments' capabilities to detect these systems, with a focus on the search for supersymmetry. As the amount of collision data increases, smaller systems like charm mesons embedded in jets are also an important area of study, and experiments are optimizing protocols for their detection. A comprehensive discussion of minor systems, including both general searches and targeted studies of supersymmetry, is presented, with an analysis of current searches using data from the Tevatron and LHC, and an examination of future detection possibilities using the HL-LHC and future colliders. This article also reviews techniques for object selection, production mechanisms, and signal and background estimation, with an emphasis on charm mesons embedded in jets. Although primarily focused on supersymmetry, this article also discusses other physics beyond the Standard Model that can be investigated using minor systems, and provides an overview of ongoing and future experimental and theoretical work in this area. This article is intended for both experienced physicists and graduate students, with an introductory focus on theoretical and experimental basics. As such, it is hoped that this article will serve as a comprehensive reference on minor systems at the LHC. This article is based on the proceedings from the 21st Cracow Epiphany Conference, held in January 2020.

A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of behavior. This study challenges that idea by revealing that the intervals between which neutron star binaries experience outbursts are not random and can be accurately predicted using a power law model. Furthermore, the team behind the study found that the majority of these occurrences fall within a specific range, specifically those 30 days or less in duration. If applied to the X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center, this finding would imply that the majority of the sources that have remained inactive for over a decade are actually stellar mass black holes. The study's results also shed new light on the nature of the sources that exhibit recurring patterns of behavior, suggesting that their outbursts can be triggered by the passage of specific orbits corresponding to the binary systems, and that the majority of these sources are actually neutron star binaries with high masses. Th thermodynamic fluctuations that occur during the propagation of acoustic waves package sound waves into "packets" that can be termed as phonons. Although phonons primarily interact with the mechanical properties of materials, their relationship with the intricate behavior of electrons is much more extensive. In matter, acoustic waves can exert a direct influence on the internal structure of atoms, causing their arrangement to change and varying depending on the speed at which they move and the direction in which they move. This, in turn, affects the bonding between atoms and consequently shapes the energy levels of atoms, varying depending on the speed and direction of motion. Understanding the meaning of conversations relies heavily on grasping the semantics of individual words, in addition to their combined semantic value within the conversation.  This variation in semantic content poses a significant challenge for models like BERT, which prioritizes concise representations.  In this research, a novel assessment of word semantics and their combined semantic content is presented, utilizing a combination of Natural Language Inference to define the semantic relationship between words in conversations.  A dedicated dataset, consisting of 20,000 NLI statements derived from conversational contexts, is introduced to evaluate the capabilities of models in capturing the variety of semantic content in conversations.  A crucial finding revealed is that the current state-of-the-art model BERT struggles with distinguishing between related words, demonstrating a limited comprehension of the semantic variety in conversations.  To address this limitation, a proposed method of model fine-tuning for NLI within conversations is presented, which significantly enhances BIRT's and BLOOFER's capacity to capture the semantic variety in conversations.  In the evaluation section, this research also introduces a new metric, the Semantic Variety Score, which evaluates the capability of models to capture the diversity of semantic content in conversations.  Overall, a comprehensive framework for assessing the capability of models to capture the variety of semantic content in conversations has been established, which can be applied to any conversation dataset protected by NLP confidentiality agreements such as Google's TOU.  This research and resulting dataset are available online at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/semantic Variety.  All related data acquisition, model training, and evaluation were conducted fairly exclusively on heavily equipped university servers.  Specifically, all experiments were carried out on 4 NVIDIA V100 16GB GPUs.  This research was funded by the NSF Intelligent Systems Center and the UC Berkeley AI Research Lab.  All conversations used in this research were randomly selected conversation instances from publicly available sources including but not limited to the internet forum website reddit.com.  All words in the conversations used in this research were labeled as described in the methodology section, which is available at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/semantic Variety.  According to the TOU of reddit.com, due permission from the original creators of the conversations used in this research has been obtained.  All conversations used in this research will be made available at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/semantic Variety.  This research was conducted in accordance with the principles of UC Berkeley's AI Research Lab's Code of Conduct, which is available at https://ai.berkeley

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative procedure for discovering such a representation and includes an analysis of its performance characteristics. Specifically, it proves that the method can handle instances where the number of nodes across the two groups differs by at most a factor of $k$ or where the maximum degree across the graph exceeds $k$ in $O(k^2 \cdot n)$ time, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes. The paper also discusses the applicability of this approach to related problems, including bipartite drawing and convex hull detection from different perspectives. The underlying algorithm's high level structure resembles a variant of the $A^*$ search algorithm using non-adaptive branching and bounding techniques. The paper provides an explicit definition of this approach and explores its connection to other problems, offering a framework that can be viewed as a problem-specific variant of the Convex Hull Problem and Bipartite Drawing Problem. The paper concludes by examining the restriction imposed by the requirement for node splitting and the limited interval between the two groups' node counts or the maximum degree and graph node count, presenting possible remedies such as ignoring this constraint or using node splitting to remove the corresponding restriction, the application of different drawing styles including edge-free representations and 2-tier layouts, the possibility of formulating the problem as a optimization problem where the objective is to minimize the number of nodes at one end of the drawing and the distance between corresponding nodes, and the potential of the approach for use in other context such as convex hull detection from different perspectives. The paper includes a brief discussion of the approach's limitations and possible future work including the investigation of more sophisticated branching strategies, the integration of the algorithm with existing force-directed methods, the exploration of different drawing styles and the investigation of new node splitting criteria. The paper also includes a detailed description of the approach and related problems including bipartite drawing

We introduce a new category called disentangled links in a certain type of enhanced knot theory, which includes classical and welded links. This category allows us to define a meaningful operation called disentanglement for links. We demonstrate that the forgetful function from classical links to disentangled links in this enhanced setting preserves the properties of volume, perimeter, and surface area. Furthermore, we find that the volume, surface area, and perimeter of disentangled links can be calculated using the same formulas used for classical links. Additionally, we establish that the surface area of a welded link can be determined by considering the surface area of a classical link that represents the same link structure. This is achieved through the application of a non-decreasing function called localization, which is an extension of the volume function used in classical link theory. This leads to the conclusion that the volume, perimeter, and surface area functions all become equivalent in the case of disentangled links. We also examine properties of disentangled links and provide a clear formula for the number of disentangled links consisting of a specified number of components and a given knot type. Furthermore, we establish that the number of disentangled links equal to a particular knot type is directly proportional to the volume of that knot type. This is a significant finding that was initially discovered by Morwen and Norris and we provide a more general proof for it. We end by exploring the relationship between volume and surface area of disentangled links and provide an alternative interpretation of the operation called disentanglement. This operation can be viewed as a way of reducing the surface area of a link while maintaining its volume, and we establish that the minimum possible reduction in surface area is equal to the volume of the link itself. This leads to the conclusion that the ratio of the surface area to the volume of a link cannot be less than 1, which is a topological equivalent of the well-known fact that the ratio of the surface area to the volume of a sphere cannot be less than 2. We also provide an alternative proof for this fact using the operation called disentanglement and explore the possibility of its application to other geometric objects. We end by examining the possibility of applying the operation called disentanglement to the study of 4-dimensional shapes, which are known as 4-manifolds. This leads to the discovery of an interesting property of the operation called disentanglement and provides an alternative interpretation of the property called additivity in the context of 4-manifolds. In complex tasks that involve simultaneous sub-tasks across different locations, a common goal is to synchronize tasks efficiently. This synchronization can be achieved by assigning tasks to locations based on their level of computation requirement, positioning them in a centralized or decentralized manner. In this work, multiple agents are tasked with performing a centralized computation at different locations, with the option to communicate with each other. The objective of the agents is to minimize their response time to a time-updated signal, undergoing random changes. To achieve this, we develop an adaptive decentralized strategy that directs data transmission towards locations where the computation is most heavily needed, without limiting the extent of its coverage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this strategy results in a minimized response time, achieving a significant improvement over randomized transmission policies. Moreover, this strategy is robust in dynamic scenarios, exhibiting a superior performance compared to centralized and decentralized alternatives. Moreover, with the presence of errors in transmission or processing, our strategy is able to adapt and minimize the impact of these errors on its performance. Lastly, simulations are conducted to validate the efficacy of this strategy in realistic scenarios. The developed approach can be applied to a wide range of applications, including those with changing environments, by incorporating maintenance and renewal processes into its framework. The use of this approach can also be expanded to other context such as scheduling and optimization problems. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both a randomized and low-dimensional feature space transformation. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Interestingly, our method proves particularly effective at processing datasets featuring non-linear relationships, as demonstrated by both simulation studies and real-world examples. In particular, our proposed approach achieves notable improvements when employing random features methods on datasets characterized by a linear relationship, as well as in scenarios requiring inductive learning. In contrast to the straight-forward implementation of RFF, our method requires a more sophisticated setup involving multiple components, including the specification of suitable random features, thresholding, and a linear combination of transformed data points. In response to these challenges, this paper provides a range of easy-to-implement approximations aimed at striking a balance between computational simplicity and statistical learning performance. In addition to these modifications, our method offers a range of useful extensions, including the ability to use pre-trained machine learning models, as well as kernel-based models employing a linear relationship. In order to maintain consistency with the original random features method, our proposed technique can be viewed as a special case of the NF2 framework, yet our results also demonstrate the significance of careful data-dependent tuning in order to achieve optimal performance. In conclusion, our proposed technique provides a versatile framework for improving the performance of machine learning algorithms using random features, as well as a range of related techniques. In order to demonstrate the practical applications of our proposed technique, we showcase its use in a range of challenging scenarios, including time-series forecasting, inductive learning, and linear relationships, in addition to providing a range of useful code snippets for programmers wishing to implement our proposed technique. In contrast to the widespread adoption of random features methods, our proposed technique provides a critical examination of the underlying assumptions, as well as a range of challenging scenarios in which our proposed technique achieves better performance

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We have obtained two primary results regarding these hypersurfaces. Firstly, under the assumption that one of these hypersurfaces has a constant M\"obius curvature and is compact, we can prove that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by a circle of a specific radius and a set of n-dimensional lines that are parallel to each other.
