A graph's edge coloring can be seen as a method to assign different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mimicking a vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was first explored by Las Vergnas in 1974. A question arising from this observation is whether there's a standard graph that can't be colored using a specific approach, known as the Ramsey property. In a previous study, it was proven that all bipartite graphs possess the Ramsey property through an edge coloring equivalent to a 2-coloring of the original graph. Consequently, a condition was established linking a graph's bipartiteness to its ability to exhibit the Ramsey property. However, this condition was recently found to be nonnecessary, uncovering a counterexample that disproves the condition's status as a necessary aspect of bipartite graphs. This paper presents an edge coloring of a specific bipartite graph that resists a certain stability standard known as cubic stability. Despite this resistance, the graph remains structurally unsensitive, and as such, its edge coloring can be considered robust. The introduced counterexample surpasses an earlier edge coloring mentioned in the paper discussions. The paper also examines the edge coloring of a specific discrete time step process. The main research question is whether there exists a standard graph that can't be colored using the mentioned edge coloring approach, known as the Ramsey property. The paper presents a specific group of graphs called cubic bipartite graphs and investigates the Ramsey property within this context. The paper also discusses another related question arising from the edge coloring transformation, known as perfectness. We propose a novel method for creating a unified multi-lingual embedding in a shared semantic space. Our approach uses a cluster-consistent word embedding to incorporate multiple perspectives of similar words across different languages, leveraging a mix of global and local optimization objectives. We employ a combination of global alignment of low-frequency words and local refinement of embedded clusters to construct a cohesive multi-lingual representation. Our approach boasts a more efficient training process and outperforms current multi-lingual embedding methods in cross-lingual lexical substitution tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate its capability in modeling linguistic properties by applying it to the analysis of embedded semantic clusters. Our method's superiority is further validated through comparisons with the multi-lingual BERT and other baseline methods in experiments conducted on four diverse language pairs. Our code has been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyangyao/CCWE.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the inclusion problem with regular expressions, taking into consideration variables representing unknown strings. These variables can be incorporated into the expressions by using union, concatenation, and star operations, as well as a new activity, specifically with variables. However, the method does not support negation over variables. Our algorithm initially offers a rough framework for addressing the problem, followed by a more refined strategy that breaks down complex issues into more manageable subtasks. We introduce a new way of representing regular expressions using Boolean expressions, and demonstrate how this representation enables us to utilize existing methods for solving Boolean equations, such as the Brzozowski algebraic method, to solve regular expression constraints. Unlike other approaches, our method can combine positive constraints using the star operation. We also show that solving the constraint that two regular expressions are unequal is equivalent to solving two inclusion constraints. Furthermore, we provide a detailed example of a complex constraint that requires a high level of abstraction, demonstrating how it can be simplified into a more manageable form. This research was conducted as part of the activity to develop the Veremos tool, which aims to provide an interactive environment for developing and testing theories related to regular expressions. This involves creating a library of predefined constraints that can be combined using the tool's combination function, as well as generating graphs from these constraints for visual analysis. This work was also presented at the 2020 ACM SIGPLAN formal research project track. The associated source code is available for public use. Additionally, we provide a preliminary investigation of a new approach related to the static analysis of programs written in a functional language that includes a monad defined using regular expressions. This investigation involves developing a way to handle variables within regular expressions, as well as a method for translating these expressions into the lambda calculus. Mobile robots and autonomous systems require efficient and robust localization techniques to navigate their environments. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide accurate and real-time orientation and position information, but their state starts unknown and drifts over time. To address these challenges, we investigate deep learning models for visual-inertial localization, specifically using IMUs and a single camera. Our proposed EMA-VIO model leverages an external memory attention mechanism to compare observed optical flows with predicted ones, thereby determining the reliability of the state. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by showing that in addition to reliable state estimation, the model can accurately determine optical flow slopes in turbulent optical flows, such as those encountered in forests. Our results indicate that in continuously changing environments, our model yields the best results among compared methods in terms of mean squared error. Furthermore, we show that in still or slowly moving environments, our model can achieve the same level of accuracy as compared methods while offering the advantage of providing flow slopes. Our code is available at https://github.com/shahpar/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, yet certain materials exhibit non-linear quantum behavior driven by cubic symmetry, not directly related to linear reciprocity. A recent study reveals that a specific compound, perovskite iron nitride, possesses the unique property of cubic symmetry and extensive wave vector clarity, therefore it should be categorized as a Weyl material, but with a square-root (not linear) topological characterisation. Researchers found that this material exhibits non-linear topological immunity to perturbations, which break wave vector clarity, and that its electronic states demonstrate looped, rather than linear, trajectories along the material's crystal structure. Furthermore, theoretical predictions placed within experimental context, have been presented, which include possible n-dimensional generalizations of this unique property, offering a broader understanding of this finding. Despite general theoretical frameworks for this property, extensive research has thus far only proven the occurrence of this feature in one specific dimension, three-dimensional $k$-space. Lastly, this study highlighted the challenging distinction of defining wave vector clarity, which is crucial for defining Weyl materials in both three-dimensional $k$-space and in one-dimensional scenarios along specific material directions. This could be achieved by utilizing a new criterion based solely on the distribution of fermion states within these materials. This state distribution based criterion provides a more stable platform for predicting the occurrence of Weyl materials, compared to wave vector clarity. This was proven by demonstrating that this new criterion remains constant even when wave vector clarity breaks down, which in turn causes the demise of Weyl materials. This research was theoretically analyzed using multiple approaches, which included nonlinear topological physics, combination of bulk and surface physics, and real-space simulations of material properties. This led to several possible experimental signatures, such as non-linear topological immunity in three-dimensional materials, the occurrence of looped trajectories in two-dimensional materials, and the unique property of square-root topological states in one-dimensional materials along specific material directions. This property can be detected using multiple experimental approaches, which included high-energy electron emission experiments, scanning tunneling microscopy, and magnetic measurement tools. This research concluded by discussing the potential of these materials in advanced technology, such as quantum computing and advanced magnetic materials, and the possible occurrence of these materials in nature, which could have significant implications for planetary science. This study opened up an exciting area of research in three-dimensional $k$-space, three-dimensional materials, and one-dimensional materials along specific material directions, which could be further developed by the scientific community. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on boundary conditions by using electric field data at an interior point and the fully observed conditions on part of the boundary. A backward Maxwell equation is introduced to transform the problem into a system of the Maxwell equations and the quasi-reversibility method is used to develop a numerical scheme to solve the problem. Key aspects of the method, including stability, convergence, and accuracy, are analyzed. A straightforward differentiation approach is used to build the numerical solution, where the uniqueness and existence of the solution are guaranteed by the Ladyzhenskaya-Shibankai and Agmon estimates. A priori error estimates are also provided to evaluate the numerical solution. A stable and convergent $O(\Delta t^2+\hdelta^2)+O(h_x^2+h_y^2)$ numerical scheme is demonstrated through various test cases, where $\Delta t$, $h_x$, $h_y$, and $\delta$ represent the time step, spatial steps in the x and y directions, and the distance between the interior point and the closest point on the observed boundary, respectively. The accuracy of the method is further validated by increasing the resolution of the spatial and temporal grids and analyzing the impact of grid size on the solution. The uniqueness of the solution can be ensured by choosing a small time step and a specific distance threshold, where the solution remains stable and the error remains small when within these parameters. The development of this numerical scheme provides a foundation for extending the reconstruction method to more complex scenarios, such as time-varying boundaries and multiple interior measurement points. We analyze the effect of extending the rational numbers from a rational base field $\Q$ with a quartic field $K$, via a Galois extension with the symmetric group $S_4$ or $A_4$, on the rank of an elliptic curve. Previously established results provide us with information on the rank increase in cases where the quartic field has a cubic resolvent, is obtained from a cubic extension of the rational numbers, or if it contains a factorable quartic equation where the discriminant is known. In these instances, the rank increase can be determined. Furthermore, we demonstrate that there are instances associated with these cases where the rank increase is greater than 2, in fact, we prove this for certain curves in the scenario of a cubic resolvent, whereas for the other scenarios, we provide theoretical evidence. In addition, we investigate the relationship between the rank increase and specific invariants of the elliptic curve, as well as its connection to the rank increase and the system of conjugate quartic fields within the extension S_4\Q. Finally, our findings extend an earlier result of Goldfeld and withdraw an earlier paper's conjecture. The proposed method also offers a clear expression that relates the rank increase to the number of quadratic extensions of the rational numbers within the S_4\Q system, from which the rank increase can be computed for individual curves. The method involves using the method of Gross and Rubinstein, combined with an alternative interpretation of their result, as well as the proposed expression provides a means of predicting the rank increase for random elliptic curves, in particular, for curves in the scenario of a cubic resolvent. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely intense laser conditions. This component can modify the polarization of laser pulses with fluences reaching PW levels and enforces a specific spatial pattern on the electric field distribution. This pattern can further support focusing laser pulses to extremely high densities not accessible with traditional optics. Our simulations demonstrate that a $4$ PW laser pulse can be completely converted from linear to circular polarization, and that the generated waveplate-induced pattern in the electric field distribution facilitates the achievement of $10^{22}$ W/cm$^2$ within a few picoseconds in a $10$ $\mu$m thick plasma, leaving a $7$ $\mu$m thick plasma layer in a solid state. This is a novel type of plasma component that can safely reach the limits of laser pulse intensity and still provide valuable information on the detailed plasma dynamics. This research was published in Physics of Plasmas, a journal of the American Institute of Physics, and is available at: https://doi.org/10.1063/5.807895.

To investigate the impact of cosmic velocity field on dark matter halo mass function, we employed a deep learning approach with a generative adversarial network. By producing a range of cosmic velocity fields with corresponding halo mass functions, we generated models of the velocity field's effect on the halo mass function. These models were tested in an experimental setup mimicking the actual universe. Our analysis of these models revealed the velocity field's impact on the halo mass function over a wide range of scales, as well as its effect on the mass function's shape, particularly its relationship with the peak height parameter. Furthermore, we extracted the velocity field's impact from observed data sets, using mock data sets with accurately recorded velocity fields, and compared the extracted effect to the actual recorded velocity fields, demonstrating a high level of accuracy. These results were achieved using a novel deep learning approach, and we also explored different formulations of the problem, including models of the velocity field's effect on the halo mass function, and compared them to the actual recorded velocity fields, demonstrating a high level of accuracy. These findings provide a solid foundation for using deep learning to investigate the velocity field's effect on the halo mass function, and can be applied to predict the velocity field's impact on the halo mass function in the actual universe, using the two-point correlation function and peak height parameter. The predicted velocity field's impact on the halo mass function was further analyzed in the actual universe, using the LOVeHDM numerical simulation, and the results were compared to the predicted velocity field's impact on the halo mass function in the $\Lambda$CDM scenario, demonstrating a noticeable discrepancy. The predicted velocity field's impact on the halo mass function was also expressed in terms of the bulk flow speed, which was further analyzed in the actual universe, using the LOVeHDM numerical simulation, and the results were compared to the predicted velocity field's impact on the halo mass function in the $\Lambda$CDM scenario, demonstrating a discrepancy of over three parsecs. The underlying assumption of a velocity field equal to zero, which is commonly used in dark matter halo mass function models, was evaluated as approximately 13 parsecs, based on the analysis of the LOVeHDM numerical simulation, which provides a more accurate representation of the actual universe. The results presented in this study were compared to the findings of an alternative approach using traditional methods, which yielded similar results, but with a scale threshold of approximately three parsecs. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. This paper introduces an innovative method to minimize the number of labels required to train high-performing document extraction models. Currently, binding rules require that each data point be carefully labeled to include both a binary classification indicating presence or absence of a specified visual element, as well as a precise bounding box to define the element's location within the document. In contrast, our approach leverages just one label per data point, classifying the document as relevant or irrelevant to the target element. Our method utilizes an unbiased, adversarial augmentation technique to generate additional training examples from existing resources, coupled with a risk-sensitive minimum empirical loss estimator to penalize excessive generalization. As a result, our approach enables significant reductions in labeling costs without sacrificing performance, as demonstrated by our results showing equivalent document extraction accuracy with just 10% of the original label set required. Moreover, our method exhibits scalability by minimizing the need for extensive data preparation, necessitating only a small group of expertly labeled documents to establish foundational knowledge. Finally, our technique shows cross-applicability to existing models by incorporating an adaptation module that seamlessly integrates with pre-trained models, thus enabling risk-sensitive training without the need for additional labeling. In total, our method yields a 90% reduction in labeling costs, according to our experiments using three distinct document extraction tasks. In particular, we used the SROIE dataset for evaluating our approach within scenarios characterized by simple layouts, resulted in an 86% reduction in labeling costs; the ICDAR dataset for evaluating our approach within scenarios characterized by complex layouts, resulted in a 88% reduction in labeling costs; and the CAMD dataset for evaluating our approach within scenarios characterized by 3D layouts, resulted in a 92% reduction in labeling costs. In addition to these findings, we discovered that our method yields favorable comparisons to existing baselines, consisting of a 24% improvement in F-score for the SROIE dataset and a 20% improvement in F-score for the ICDAR dataset. In conclusion, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing labeling costs without sacrificing performance, coupled with the versatility of our method in addressing diverse document extraction tasks. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, entitled WaveNet, and highlight the challenges faced and potential improvements. Given the expected rate of detections for future LIGO-like detectors, we also explore methods to enhance the efficiency of this network in real-time applications. Ultimately, this deep learning framework has the potential to maximize the detection efficiency of neutron star and black hole binaries in real-time, across a wide range of signals, and on various detector platforms similar to LIGO. We conclude by examining the scope for enhancing WaveNet and integrating it with existing electromagnetic observation protocols. If you would like to try WaveNet, you can access the code at https://github.com/ResNets/WaveNet.

Social distancing measures implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic significantly reduced urban encounters, leading to diverse speculations about their effect on income diversity. This study analyzes public places' social interaction data collected in Tokyo, Japan before and during the pandemic to examine the income diversity of these interactions. Previous data shows that the income diversity of Tokyo's public places ranks high globally. However, our findings indicate that the pandemic-related reduction in public gatherings resulted in a less diverse range of incomes among the people interacting in these spaces. This change became more pronounced over time as the pandemic continued, and we observed similar trends among various age groups. Interestingly, the pandemic's impact on income diversity did not change significantly across different age groups in our data. This study's results suggest that reducing social distancing measures may help increase the income diversity of urban encounters but also highlights the underlying factors contributing to this decline, including the income heterogeneity of people's home neighborhoods or their willingness to visit public places outside their local area. By taking these factors into account, we can hope to restore the pre-pandemic level of income diversity in urban encounters. However, unlike lower-mass protostars, massive protostars experience significant pressure forces due to their substantial mass, which prevents them from accelerating downward into the cloud. This pressure acceleration is directed upward, enabling these stars to move through the cloud at their own pace. As a result, their surrounding environments are likely distinct from the dense clouds they originally formed from. This process can also be identified by looking for groups of stars that have formed at the same time in the same location, and that share similar compositions, as indicated by analyzing the elements present in the stars and the materials surrounding them. In this proof, a modified version of Stokes' formula in differential forms is demonstrated for a locally convex space without the requirement of compactness. To achieve this, the method involves utilizing the Hahn-Banach theorem to establish an extension of the divergence operator, making it possible to apply Stokes' formula to forms with locally bounded derivatives. A subsequent section shows that this approach can be naturally applied to establish a fundamental result in the theory of partial differential equations, specifically the uniqueness of solutions derived from the first approach, which is applicable in the context of distributions. Another section is dedicated to examining the concept of differential shapes, which are defined as locally defined surfaces with differentiable normal vectors, and demonstrates how they can be utilized to demonstrate Stokes' formula for distributional derivatives without the constraint of working on a compact domain. A final section explores the relationship between differential shapes and locally compact surfaces, and presents an alternative proof of the uniqueness of the solution derived from the distributional approach. A note at the end discusses potential generalizations of this method. A special mention is also given to the prior work of several authors on this subject, including the contributions of Colombeau, Schlenker, and the combination of the latter with the method of distributions. A brief overview of these approaches can be found in the epilogue section. A glossary is provided to clarify the meaning of various terms used in this context, including the definition of differential shapes, surfaces, normal vectors, and distributions. A list of the main theorems demonstrated in this proof is presented as Theorem 1 through Theorem 9 in the theorem section, which includes both the unique solution and the compact domain results, as well as several other important statements on the convergence of forms, the properties of distributional derivatives, and the relationship between surfaces and normal vectors. A special section dedicated to the concept of differential shapes also exists in the appendix section, which includes additional information on locally defined surfaces, normal vectors, and the relationship between them, as well as a characterization of surfaces defined by normal vectors in the context of distributions. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, specifically the limitations of large-scale pre-trained language models like BERT, as well as opportunities for further innovation in the realm of fake news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/AhmedHamdy1991/CMTR-BERT.

This research investigates the concept of a bending effect, initially observed in Gaussian random field models, which demonstrates that a minimum level of local dimensionality is reached when the local variance of a field exceeds a certain threshold. Our study analyzes this phenomenon across three scenarios characterized by fixed, changing, or non-existent minimum levels of local dimensionality. The bending effect's impact on the number of significant variables is particularly notable in models where the local dimensionality does not reach a minimum, causing the number of significant variables to stabilize at zero. Our main finding also reveals that the number of significant variables can be accurately estimated using a scaling exponent related to the fraction of explainable variance. Additionally, we propose an alternative interpretation of the bending effect in the context of Gaussian random fields, viewing it as a local variance-based approach to determine the number of significant variables. This perspective facilitates the use of Gaussian random field methods for modeling non-Gaussian distributions. Our research includes a theoretical analysis of bending effect scenarios, supported by numerical examples using Gaussian random field models and a comparison with the LASSO method using synthetic data. When analyzing data that contains a dependent direction, traditional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) may fail to effectively capture the underlying structure. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring strategies for dependent-dimensional PCA, with rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-PCA being a promising approach. This method finds the data's most relevant component under the $\ell_1$-norm, while being insensitive to the orientation of that component. In this paper, a specific variant of rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-PCA is examined, and a linearly convergent optimization algorithm is proposed to solve this problem. The algorithm's effectiveness is supported by theoretical evidence, and its performance is compared to other state-of-the-art methods through simulated data and real-world applications. The results show that this algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of recovery accuracy and robustness. The development of a fast and robust optimization algorithm for rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-PCA through a majorization-and-approximation framework can also handle non-strongly convex objectives and complex models, making it a highly versatile tool for a wide range of applications. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, as model size increases, their dependence on high-quality data has intensified, rendering their underlying annotations increasingly desirable. This paper focuses on emotion-related annotated data, which is critically in need of expansion. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative method of generating new annotations from existing ones. During this process, we establish a set of guidelines to evaluate existing annotations and identify those that require revision. Next, we leverage BERT to classify mislabeled examples and rectify the annotations of difficult cases. Our proposed framework has been put to the test on a dataset consisting of annotated statements regarding emotions, mood, and social relationships. The resulting expanded dataset has been compared to a naturally expanding baseline, and our method has demonstrated significant improvements in multiple evaluation metrics. Our code is now available for public use at https://github.com/ghru/semantic-annotation-correction.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel navigation map representation featuring interconnected circular layers to represent a robot's surroundings. Each circular layer corresponds to a distinct distance range from the robot, with higher layers mapping to more distant areas. We have implemented a method allowing the robot to determine the closest map node to its current location based on its position and the distance to the node, taking into consideration the uncertainty of its location. By utilizing this method, the robot can prioritize exploring areas represented by closer map nodes, thereby focusing its search efforts on the map layers most relevant to its immediate surroundings. Through simulated trials in HiTMap, we observed a significant decrease in navigation efficiency compared to random searching. Additionally, we have incorporated an path-planning functionality into the system, which generates a route to the closest unexplored node based on the representation of its location and the map environment. We have also developed a way for the robot to validate the accuracy of its location by comparing it against the map generated from its sensor readings, which in turn allows it to update the map correctly. We have tested and compared our method to other mapping algorithms in simulation, achieving the highest success rate in navigating through unfamiliar environments. We have implemented HiTMap on a real robot, which successfully navigated and mapped an office environment, and demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by intentionally misleading it to test the accuracy of its location validation system. We have further analyzed the current limitations of HiTMap and have identified potential future improvements to the system. We have made HiTMap available openly for public use. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging to achieve with object-based programming models.  This limitation stems from object-based programming's natural suitability, which can lead to inefficient memory usage, suboptimal data arrangement, and poorly aligned memory access.  To overcome this obstacle, researchers suggest using object-based programming on SIMD devices for deeper insight into numerical applications and simpler code development.  To facilitate this, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel, dynamic memory allocator tailored for GPU object-based programming.  This allocator employs a binary tree to manage memory blocks and provides four distinct memory management functions, each finely tuned to meet the requirements of various numerical applications.  We further introduce a novel, simple method for aligning memory access within the allocator, allowing for efficient memory usage and minimal performance overhead.  DynaSOAr outperforms existing memory allocators and shows significant performance gains in various numerical applications, including linear algebra and sparse matrix operations.  We also provide comprehensive implementation details and source code for DynaSOAr, inviting further collaboration and customization.  In particular, this work is suitable for a broad range of numerical applications, including general-purpose, specially designed algorithms, and complex applications involving multiple memory allocation tasks.  To validate our findings, we conducted rigorous testing across multiple GPU platforms and discovered that DynaSOAr delivers consistent performance improvements and general applicability, offering a scalable and versatile memory allocator that can be easily integrated into a wide range of numerical applications.  We further explore DynaSOAr's capabilities on a newly introduced GPU platform and detail our testing methodology in the appendix.  In addition to DynaSOAr, we developed a simple, object-based implementation of the well-known Conjugate Gradient numerical algorithm, which serves as a basic object-based application suitable for analysis and comparison across different programming models and GPUs.  This implementation allows for varying levels of object-based programming, including both simple and complex definitions, and includes performance results for each level on a range of GPUs. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn nanoclusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. Furthermore, investigations of nanoclusters revealed YSR state interactions with the ferromagnetic interface magnetization, demonstrating magnetic field-dependent behavior. These findings yielded a comprehensive understanding of YSR states induced by magnetic impurities on a superconducting surface and the corresponding magnetic boundary interaction. A proposed model also highlighted the significance of scalar relativistic effects on the YSR states and the inherent similarity between this system and that of magnetic atoms or clusters on a normal metal. Experimental data, including low-energy electron loss spectra and magnetic hysteresis loops for clusters, were used to validate the theoretical findings, which provide a precise framework for analyzing YSR states and their properties in various systems. A related appendix is also presented which discusses the implications of this theory for Mn adatoms and nanoclusters on the Ni(111) surface based on low-energy electron loss spectra. A comparative analysis with experimental data revealed the complex magnetic behavior of Ni(111) surfaces despite its apparent simplicity, which may be attributed to the interplay between interface magnetism and the YSR states induced by the adatoms or nanoclusters. A proposed approach to investigate this interplay using advanced techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy and low-energy electron loss spectroscopy is discussed. We investigated the electronic and magnetic framework of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO$_{2}$ using a quantum-kernel hybrid DFT method. Our analysis indicates that both elements can form stable dopants with unique properties. A carbon-doped bond lengthens slightly, potentially allowing it to reside further inside the crystal structure, whereas a nitrogen-doped bond shortens and could facilitate greater interaction with the surrounding electrons. Notably, we found both types of doped bonds can exist in a semi-bridged state, extending the range of possible angles to 60-90 degrees, and demonstrating a preference for the 80 degree angle often optimal in solar cells technology. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, a phenomenon supported by core mass function data.  Furthermore, the mass of cores associated with outflows exceed the outflow mass by a factor of 10, indicating that core mass serves as the determining factor in outflow formation, rather than outflow mass in relation to core mass.  Additionally, a separate group of outflow-associated cores with low mass and veiled nearby young stellar objects are likely preprotostellar cores.  These preprotostellar cores are found within a specific mass range that, when combined with the data from protostellar and starless cores, suggests a pattern of core mass evolution.  However, this pattern differs from the conventional view, with core mass increasing rather than remaining constant or decreasing.  This notion is supported by the location of these cores at a greater distance from known sunless cores, implying that core mass may also play a significant role in determining the likelihood of sunless cores giving rise to massive star formation.  The possible connection between core mass and the likelihood of massive star formation is further underscored by the fact that only the most massive cores at the cloud's edge are associated with outflows.  The possible explanations for the observed pattern of core mass increase include the influence of magnetic turbulence or the effect of core-protopoplanet interaction.  The proprotoplanetary scenario is particularly relevant, given the presence of small dusty objects nearby some of the cores and the fact that only the most massive cores at the cloud's edge are associated with outflows.  The evidence presented here is consistent with a hypothesis that massive star formation arises from dense cores with mass greater than 50 solar masses, located at a distance from sunless cores, rather than directly originating from those cores.  The proposed hypothesis may have implications for the understanding of massive star formation in infrared dark clouds. We develop a new method to address a broad spectrum of problems involving linear random processes on the sphere, specifically including spatial signal recovery, spatial deconvolution, and spectral denoising, among others. This method relies on an innovative one-step recurrence formula that recovers a cleaned version of a signal's component from its observed, noisy counterpart. We derive this formula using a least squares approach and estimate its effectiveness using the mean squared error criterion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in comparison to traditional approaches via numerical experiments. Our results show that the proposed recurrence-based method outperforms the conventional approach based on the minimum resolution principle for most experiments. However, the outcome depends heavily on the signal's smoothness and the resolution matrix's properties. We also introduce a nonlinear recurrence formula to address cases where the signal contains singularities. This non-linear version leads to better results when compared to the linear version, especially for noisy spherical data of moderate resolution. We apply the method to clean a sphere's algebraic surface derived from Monte Carlo methods and demonstrate its resilience in removing noise from globally defined scalar fields on the sphere. We conclude that this method offers a valuable alternative to the minimum resolution principle and provides a starting point for further research into nonlinear recurrence formulas, including those for time-dependent random fields on the sphere. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghra/RecurrencesOnTheSphere.

In neural machine translation, generating text can be seen as a sequential process, one word at a time. Current methods translate words independently, without considering the overall effectiveness. This approach may lead to suboptimal results, especially when target words have different translation probabilities for the same source context. To address this, we introduce a novel focus mechanism, allocating different amounts of attention to the source sequence for different target words. By taking the target language's current state into account, we can weight the attention differently, resulting in higher translation quality. Experiments on large dataset translations show a significant improvement in BLEU scores, with a particular advantage in challenging mountainous terrain domains like technical abstraction translations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-tf.

A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. This paper focuses on analyzing plasma parameters in this plasma source, particularly in the helicon mode, where a high level of ionization is achieved through electron cyclotron resonance. Measurements of plasma properties such as plasma density, temperature, and electric potential were conducted using a range of diagnostic tools including laser fluorescence, Langmuir probes, and a neutral particle analyzer. Plasma density was confirmed to be extremely high, with values peaking at 10^20 per cubic meter, and showed excellent agreement with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the facility has been successfully operating in the helicon mode for several years, and has been used to investigate wave launch, as well as how plasma interacts with the helical antenna. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions is challenging due to the absence of suitable golden standards. In this paper, a novel W-Net framework is presented, comprising a initial feature extraction stage using convolutional neural networks and a follow-up stage involving a U-Net that refines the output of the first stage. By utilizing a low-resolution image, the network also achieves efficient count results, thereby further differentiating it from conventional U-Net-based solutions. The evaluation of the proposed method was performed on two separate datasets, namely the LUNA16 dataset containing lung tissue samples and the CVC colony dataset comprised of colorectal tissue samples. On these datasets, the proposed method demonstrated strong performance in terms of accuracy, while also showing a close correlation with the gold-standard standards used for diagnosis. In particular, the results showed an overall score of 0.78 in lung tissue samples and an F-score of 0.78 in colorectal tissue samples. In both cases, a simple approach was used for evaluation, involving the comparison of segmented cells with the corresponding regions marked by pathologists, thereby highlighting the reliability of the proposed method. In addition, the proposed evaluation method was demonstrated to be effective in detecting errors in false negatives, where cells were either misclassified as background or missed entirely. In this paper, a novel tool was also introduced, namely the False Negative Detector, intended to assist users in identifying areas where the network fails to detect individual cells. In conclusion, the challenges associated with cancer diagnosis were described, followed by the presentation of the W-Net framework, along with the proposed evaluation method. In both cases, the challenges were further compounded by the limited amount of data available for training, along with the presence of noisy data, along with the time-consuming nature of gold-standard standards, along with the complex structure of individual cells. Nevertheless, the results obtained demonstrated the effectiveness of the W-Net framework, as well as the proposed evaluation method, along with the False Negative Detector, in accurately segmenting cells, along with the detection of noisy data and the complex structure of individual cells, along with the validation of the results through comparison with gold-standard standards. The local exchange theorem is a significant concept initially developed for classical groups, providing a meaningful interpretation of certain L-functions obtained from automorphic forms on these groups. This theorem has been extensively utilized in various applications, such as the central value conjecture and the pole conjecture, both of which involve L-functions of automorphic forms. Initially established for GL2 by Langlands, the local exchange theorem was subsequently generalized to certain non-classical groups, including SO2n+1 and Sp2n+1, under certain assumptions about the characteristic of the underlying field. However, in these general cases, the assumption that the characteristic of the field is greater than 2 is necessary. This paper shows that this assumption can be relaxed, thereby extending the local exchange theorem to a broader range of situations. Specifically, the paper proves that the local exchange theorem is valid when the characteristic of the field is 2, and it also establishes a modified version of the theorem for fields of characteristic 2 with specific properties. Moreover, this extension is achieved without relying on the assumption of minimal vectors, which are a crucial component of the original proof for certain types of Shimura varieties. Instead, the paper utilizes alternative methods based on the Kottwitz--Rapoport formula and the local exchange theorem for GL2. This extension of the local exchange theorem has significant implications for certain conjectures related to L-functions, including the central value conjecture and the pole conjecture, both of which involve certain L-functions of automorphic forms on SO2n+1 and Sp2n+1. Specifically, these conjectures predict the existence of a specific pole at the central point of the corresponding L-function, which in turn is linked to the existence of certain geometric objects, namely certain components of the zero fiber of the Kottwitz--Rapoport map. This extension of the local exchange theorem provides a way to verify these conjectures for a broad range of situations, including fields of characteristic 2. Deep Neural Network techniques, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained remarkable precision in tackling complex graph-level classifications and predictions. However, the underlying mathematical principles of GCNNs, particularly with regard to their connection to linear filtering concepts, remain unclear to many researchers. This study acts as a foundational explanation of GCNNs, providing a new perspective on these networks grounded in linear filtering theory. We demonstrate that each GCNN operation can be viewed as a linear filtering operation, with the filter's structure offering valuable insights into the impact of node representation, aggregation weights, and recombination processes on GCNN outputs. The simple, intuitive framework of linear filtering in GCNNs enables easier analysis and optimization of network performance. Furthermore, this framework serves as a prerequisite for investigating more sophisticated GCNN models, such as Differential Equation GCNN, Geometric GCNN, and Dynamic GCNN. We also discuss various GCNN evaluation metrics in terms of filtering properties, presenting a comprehensive analysis of GCNN's precision. Finally, this study is applied to a renowned real-world dataset, with results showing significant improvements in precision. In a three-dimensional spacetime, a formalism is established which redefines gravitational and scalar field interactions in terms of Chern-Simons actions. This formulation serves as the basis for an alternative description of general relativity and a specific scalar field theory. It yields explicit expressions for the metric and scalar field components in terms of Chern-Simons connections, allowing for an invariant interpretation. This conversion method is particularly useful as it conveys the principles of the theory in a concise and explicit manner. It also enables an easy transition between geometrical and field-theoretical descriptions of the theory. Furthermore, this formulation facilitates an understanding of the conserved charges associated with the theory through the use of Chern-Simons coefficients. It is demonstrated that certain conditions can be met by adjusting the Chern-Simons coefficients, which in the original field-theoretical framework would require the adjustment of counterterms. This proposal can be applied to both asymptotically flat spacetimes and those with a cosmological constant. It even extends to theories with gauge fields by incorporating a U(2) Chern-Simons action, which results in the presence of monopole fields in spacetimes with hair. It is demonstrated that the rotation velocity profile of solitons and the ergosphere radius of black holes can be determined through the use of Chern-Simons connections, which also enable the interpretation of these geometrical objects in the original field-theoretical framework. This leads to the discovery that the formation of solitons and black holes with hair relies on the composition of the matter field, as well as the value of the cosmological constant. It is demonstrated that the interaction between solitons and black holes with hair occurs when the rotation velocity profile of solitons and the ergosphere radius of black holes coincide, which marks a unstable phase of the system. It is further demonstrated that the distribution of matter field fields around solitons and black holes with hair can be determined through the composition of the Chern-Simons coefficients, which also enables the calculation of the mass and charge of these objects. It is shown that solitons and black holes with hair are stable when the value of the Chern-Simons action is below a certain critical value, whereas they become unstable when the value of the Chern-Simons action exceeds this critical value. It is demonstrated that the change in the value of the Chern-Simons action controls the transition from solitons to black holes with hair, as well as the formation of solitons and black holes with hair from the vacuum spacetime

This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that there is an inherent relationship between algorithms and proofs, which can be represented through the lens of logical pseudocodes. Furthermore, this framework provides a means for deriving executions or executions trees from the perspective of natural deduction steps, which in turn can be combined into a single execution tree marking the relationships between natural deduction steps and the corresponding states in the execution tree. Our results also include a decision-making procedure regarding whether a given state is valid in the context of a given execution tree, which is achievable by examining the structure of the execution tree. We further introduce execution graphs as a natural extension to execution trees, which can be derived from natural deduction formulas with multiple conclusions. In the context of data analysis, a variation of the $k$-centers problem is often utilized to create a simplified representation of complex data sets. This problem involves identifying the minimum number of points needed to fairly divide a given dataset based on a specified property, in addition to determining the corresponding decision regions. This task can be seen as a combination of clustering and a property-defined partitioning problem. The objective of this study is to develop a a a simple and efficient algorithm that can solve the high-dimensional $k$-centers problem in a dynamic setting, where the data set and the property in question can change over time. The key innovation of this research involves creating a framework that utilizes a particular sorting method to solve clustering problems that can be solved by a specific model of a learning algorithm. The resulting algorithm of this research has a significant advantage over existing approaches for dynamic data sets, and its performance can be accurately captured by a specific growth function that reflects its computational complexity. We introduce a novel type of stochastic chase-evasion games on structured objects, incorporating separate hierarchical representations of the environment and the players' abilities. Our key contribution involves developing a universal decomposition framework for these games, incorporating multiple hierarchical models. We demonstrate the versatility of this framework by applying it to a specific type of hierarchy, and in doing so, we derive a concise algorithm to determine the winner of the game. The hierarchical decompositions we employ are constructed by dividing the marked graph representing the game's permissions and obligations into distinct, independent components. Our research also explores the relationship between these hierarchical decompositions and possible strategy trajectories, which we represent as hierarchical marked graphs. The process of converting these two types of hierarchies between each other is a crucial aspect of our work, and it is facilitated by a dedicated conversion algorithm. The resulting solution can further be optimized to accommodate dynamic changes in the game's environment. The comprehensive hierarchy we derive can be utilized to provide domain-specific insights, such as the identification of reachable places, the determination of victory states, and the validation of correct agent behavior. The methodology we developed and the associated algorithm can be applied to a variety of stochastic chase-evasion games on hierarchical structures, including those defined using Region Graphs, Time-elapsed Hierarchies, and Hierarchies of Reachable Places. The theoretical aspects of our work are accompanied by an accompanying example of a simple game, as well as two more complex case studies involving large-scale, real-world environments. The first real-world example is related to the analysis of a hierarchical network of the OSHM mine, which was the subject of a previous research paper, whereas the second real-world example involves the chase-evasion game at the NASA's Independent Verification and Validation facility. The methodology we developed and the associated algorithm can further be extended to provide a framework for solving other types of stochastic games on hierarchical structures. The research paper at hand was previously presented at the Symposium on Theory of Algorithms and Models for Natural Language Processing, which took place in May 2021. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing the posterior distribution of all possible images. We propose a new algorithm that generates a parameter space where the conditional GAN can produce high-quality samples that follow the desired posterior distribution. The proposed method produces a compact representation of the posterior distribution by incorporating a sparse regularization technique, resulting in a set of distinct samples that capture the posterior's key characteristics and differ specifically in the region where the prior constraints are ambiguous. We validate our method on multiple inverse problems and show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing techniques in terms of the quality of the samples generated. We also provide a free software for this task called the Regularized Conditional GAN, available online. We apply this method to compute the posterior distribution in a simple MRI inverse problem and compare it to an alternative reconstruction method, finding that the proposed algorithm accurately models the posterior distribution and generates reconstructed images that are consistent with the ground truth images. We also analyze the proposed algorithm's theoretical properties and show that the regularized conditional GAN produces samples that follow the desired posterior distribution, assuming that the underlying model meets certain conditions. We make some adjustments to the algorithm and show that it can handle model mispecification, resulting in samples that follow the desired posterior distribution as the number of samples increases. We conduct an extensive experimental analysis of the proposed algorithm on multiple inverse problems and compare it to existing techniques, finding that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms the baseline methods in terms of the quality of the samples generated. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through an innovative pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing a deeply cascaded autoregressive architecture, yet its limited pitch control results from converting cached states into zero-padding. To overcome this constraint, we propose a flexible Conv-TDNN-based model with pitch-dependent expanded convolutional layers, where the PDCs are conditioned on the model's internal pitch estimate. This conditionally adaptive design allows for multiple quasi-periodic states to be generated and mixed, effectively expanding the model's spectral expansion ability and enhancing the naturalness of generated samples. Evaluations using the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate that QPNet yields natural generated samples at multiple pitches without additional training, while a model trained on a broader pitch range demonstrates only a minimal improvement in results. These findings suggest that the limited pitch control of WN is sufficient for a wide range of vocalistic sounds, including speech. Code is available at: https://github.com/Parandosean/QPNet.

We have created a dataset specifically tailored to examine this challenge and explore the relationship between noise patterns and the ability to perform localization. Our findings show that deep learning models like resnets and efficient nets can successfully perform this task, while traditional methods like SVD and LVA are consistently unsuccessful. We have also implemented a simple enhancement called spatial attention, which significantly boosts the performance of both deep learning models and traditional methods in resolving this difficult task. This research is an extension of an earlier study and our code is available for public use.

We introduce LDGN - a novel GNN model that effortlessly handles Lorentzian distance and seamlessly integrates with various appointment techniques, thereby enhancing the capability of GNNs in tasks utilizing a Lorentzian distance metric. We further investigate the theoretical aspects of LDGN and demonstrate its connection to the neighborhood aggregation framework, in addition to deriving an explicit lower bound for the learning capacity of LDGN. In a comprehensive set of experiments, we validate the performance of LDGN on real-world datasets, with the findings indicating that LDGN consistently outperforms existing GNN models in tasks utilizing a Lorentzian distance metric. Moreover, we explore the applicability of LDGN to various scenarios, including the localization problem, resource allocation, and category prediction, without any additional modifications. The code for LDGN is publicly available at https://github.com/xuqing06/LDGN.

Using advanced neural styling tools for photo editing, we investigate the potential risks they pose to trusting medical diagnostics based on X-ray images. To explore this concern, we developed a working framework to artificially create synthetic X-ray images depicting lung illness symptoms, by editing normal X-ray images. This framework leverages a combination of a U-Net generator, a StyleGAN generator, and a discriminator, trained on a large dataset including images of lung illnesses and normal X-rays, with associated attribute labels. We evaluated this method on publicly available datasets and found it successfully created synthetic images that confuse human radiologists, demonstrating a connection between editing risks and the quality of the generated images. This evaluation enables the development of robust neural editing tools that minimize synthetic image creation effectiveness, a novel assessment approached through the use of a simple gaming-like model by human radiologists, which prioritizes clinical reality. This work paves the way for multiple potential applications, including verifying the reliability of neural editing tools, assessing photo editing safety for medical diagnostics, and developing methods to distinguish real from synthetic X-ray images depicting lung illnesses. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and in-depth examination, designed to accommodate user-created scripts for custom operations and calculations. The tool, tailored for user interaction, enables efficient exploration of large datasets by performing operations such as component separation, conversion between data representations, and component transformation. The application also features an integrated editor for creating and editing scripts, which can be visually represented and easily understood due to the detailed display of variables, functions, and calculations. A distinctive aspect of ViDaExpert is its capacity to create interactive modules for complex tasks that can be carried out directly within the application, without the need for additional programming. The application is particularly well-suited for handling issues like dimensionality reduction, where it can efficiently handle challenging algorithms like t-SNE, by providing real-time visual updates during the calculation process. The development of ViDaExpert focused on simplicity and ease of use, resulting in an intuitive interface that minimizes the need for manual coding and allows users to concentrate on data analysis rather than programming. The application is capable of handling large datasets and features a robust editor for creating and editing scripts, along with multiple visualization options including scatter plots, layering, and link maps. ViDaExpert is primarily designed for the visualization of metadata that accompanies high-dimensional data, rather than the analysis of text-based data. The application is available for free use or custom modification under the GPL v2 license. The ViDaExpert application is tailored to operate with datasets composed of vectors, cannot handle integer-based algorithms like k-Means, and is capable of integrating with the R programming environment for the creation of custom scripts. The development of ViDaExpert was driven by the need for an intuitive and easily extensible visualization tool that could efficiently handle complex algorithms and provide detailed data analysis capabilities. The application can be used for general-purpose data analysis tasks, was used in the analysis of high-dimensional data related to the visualization of genomic sequences, and examples of its usage in such contexts are presented in the accompanying documents. The development of ViDaExpert also led to the creation of methods for the reduction of complex high-dimensional data, specifically the t-SNE layering method and the ViDaExpert dimension reduction algorithm. The application is available for free download from the specified website. The t-SNE layering method is distinct from other t-SNE implementations as it prioritizes the preservation of global patterns and allows for the reduction of high-dimensional data without the loss of important features, achieved through the use of multiple t-SNE layers and the selection of optimal parameters.
